solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicatorNotes.part in: the answer is a part lying within the words that follow

annotation.surface: A note on which actor plays the lead in Shelley's verse drama.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Star' reads as a leading actor in Shelley's play, and it is the astronomical kind; the answer spans the gap between the two words of the title.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: our Sun is the nearest example of a star.

blocks.note: the rhythmic accent that falls on a syllable in a line of verse
to push a point hard so nobody can miss it

annotation.surface: A harassed commuter getting past their nerves and driving back from work.
annotation.walkthrough: Three definitions, not two: 'drive home' is a third meaning, not a journey after work.
annotation.definitionFit: A triple definition: the accent in a verse line, mental strain, and emphasising a point all share the word.

entries.clue: What drawers are filled with pounds? (6)

annotation.definition: What drawers are filled with pounds?

blocks.note: the surface pushes a chest of drawers; the setter means underwear, and the word for that holds a shorter word inside it
British slang for pounds sterling, the same word singular or plural, like 'quid'

annotation.surface: A question about a chest of drawers stuffed with cash.
annotation.walkthrough: The drawers are underwear, KNICKERS, not furniture; NICKER is British slang for a pound (plural also 'nicker'), and it fills the word KNICKERS.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: a pound sterling is a nicker, and the word sits inside KNICKERS, the underwear the clue calls drawers.

blocks.note: the pen name of Aurore Dupin, 19th-century French novelist and lover of Chopin
what a desert dune is heaped up from

annotation.surface: A literary critic tracing Frank Herbert's novel back to a French writer.
annotation.walkthrough: Dune's capital letter points at the novel, but it is only a sand dune.
annotation.definitionFit: A pen name and a plain material: Aurore Dupin wrote as George Sand, and desert dunes are built of blown grains.

entries.clue: Suspect something fishy about a prolific run scorer (5,1,3)

indicatorNotes.about: the fish goes around the batsman

blocks.note: a smelt is a small fish
Brian Lara, the West Indies batsman who holds the Test record score

annotation.surface: Doubts about a cricketer who scores too many runs to be honest.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Something fishy' looks like part of the definition, suspecting something fishy; it is a literal fish. Brian Lara is the West Indian cricketer who scored 400 not out in a Test.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to smell a rat means to sense that some trickery is afoot, the same as to suspect.

indicatorNotes.bananas: bananas = crazy, so the letters go mad

annotation.surface: A tree's crown described as utterly crazy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crown, say' looks like an example of a tree's top, and the words are only letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Norway spruce is a European conifer, the traditional Christmas tree.

entries.clue: Boyfriends left more than heart in Cisco (6)

indicatorNotes.heart in: the heart of a word is its middle letter

annotation.surface: Boyfriends who took more than someone's heart when they left San Francisco.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cisco' reads like a nickname for San Francisco, where hearts are famously left; it is only there to give its middle letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a boyfriend is one partner in a romance, one of a pair of lovers.

entries.clue: Drawing off the last of what is due (5)

indicatorNotes.off: the letter comes off the word

blocks.note: towing = drawing, as a car draws a trailer
the last letter of whaT, removed

annotation.surface: A sketch taken off the wall to pay the last of a debt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' pretends to be a picture; it means pulling, as in towing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a debt still to be paid is both owing and due.

entries.clue: Sort of field chosen to cut down cereal (8)

indicatorNotes.cut down: the word is cut short, losing its last letter

annotation.surface: A farmer choosing which field to clear of its cereal crop.
annotation.walkthrough: The farm field is really the physics one, an electric field.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: physics has electric, magnetic and gravitational fields, and the clue asks for one sort.

annotation.surface: A travel agent's advice on how early to book a cheap trip.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead time' reads as one phrase, the notice needed to book; the two words work separately.
annotation.definitionFit: A historical sense: steerage was the cheapest class of passage on an ocean liner.

entries.clue: Film about vectors, regularly shown in ballistics (8)

indicatorNotes.about: the film goes around the letters

annotation.surface: A film about the maths of trajectories, as used in ballistics.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all physics, vectors and trajectories, and the film is a boxing one.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: the science of launching rockets is a branch of ballistics, the study of projectiles in flight.

indicatorNotes.after: the study comes after the ridicule

annotation.surface: A study dropped after it was mocked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb, dropping a study; it is a cut of beef.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ribeye is one cut of beef, taken from the rib section.

annotation.surface: Halting investment in the social network X.
annotation.walkthrough: X reads as the company, and it is just the letter X written as a capital.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: X written as a plain upper-case letter is one instance of the answer.

blocks.note: a stretch or period, as in a cold snap lasting a while
to signify or foretell, as when dark clouds promise rain

annotation.walkthrough: 'Time signal' reads as the radio pips; the two words are separate definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a stretch of time, as in a dry spell, and signalling, as when clouds spell rain.

entries.clue: Predator’s trail disguised with a log (9)

indicatorNotes.disguised: the letters are disguised by being rearranged

annotation.surface: A hunter's track hidden by a log across it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is almost the answer's own picture: an alligator lying still looks like a log.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the alligator is an ambush predator of American swamps.

blocks.note: to press clothes is to smooth them

annotation.surface: A slick, snide item pasted into someone's scrapbook.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smooth, sarcastic' reads as a description of a person; each adjective works alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an article clipped from a newspaper is the classic thing pasted into a scrapbook.

indicatorNotes.fragments: steel breaks into fragments, scattering its letters

blocks.note: to cope is to get by

annotation.surface: Bits of a steel meteorite that make it through a shower of shooting stars.
annotation.walkthrough: A meteor shower is a burst of shooting stars, but here a 'shower' is something that shows, so the meteor shower shows you meteors.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun: read as 'meteor show-er', something that shows you meteors, which an astronomer's instrument does.

blocks.note: a scab forms as skin heals
bar = saving, except, as in 'bar none'

annotation.surface: A duke's wounded swordsman being nursed back to health.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sword-bearer' suggests the duke's attendant, but it is the sheath that holds the sword.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful description: the sheath that carries, or bears, a sword is its bearer.

blocks.note: a suit is a lawsuit, argued in court
a case is what a court tries

annotation.surface: Two quarrels over checking whether a bag will fit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trying' is legal, trying a case in court, and both SUIT and CASE are legal actions heard there.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the travelling bag for clothes is one piece of luggage.

entries.clue: A cat could run wild being thirsty for blood (5,7)

indicatorNotes.wild: wild letters are out of control and out of order

annotation.surface: A cat roaming feral and hungry for the kill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Run wild' looks like one phrase; 'run' belongs to the letters and 'wild' alone scrambles them.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Bram Stoker's vampire is a being who craves blood.

entries.clue: Is inconsistent duck dropped by egg producers? (6)

indicatorNotes.dropped by: the O is dropped by the longer word

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so O

annotation.surface: Farmers wondering why their hens drop eggs so erratically.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Egg producers' suggests hens; it is the anatomy. A duck is a zero score in cricket, so it gives O.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that keeps changing does not stay the same, so it is inconsistent.

annotation.surface: An environmental protester storming a school biology lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Classes' are school lessons in the surface and taxonomic groups in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: biologists classify species into groups ranked just above them, and 'classes' stands for such groups in general.

entries.clue: Bloomer, primarily curved, flatter round the sides (9)

indicatorNotes.primarily: 'primarily' means first of all, so take the first letter
indicatorNotes.round the sides: the phrase wraps round the letter at both sides

blocks.note: to butter up is to flatter

annotation.surface: A loaf of bread, curved and flattened at the sides.
annotation.walkthrough: A bloomer is a British loaf of bread, which the surface describes; here it is something that blooms.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun: a bloomer is anything that blooms, and this yellow meadow flower is one.

indicatorNotes.ending to: the ending of a word is its last letter

annotation.surface: A comedian's tired stock punchline.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stock' reads as an adjective, a stock ending; it is the verb, to stock or supply.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to stock a kitchen or a ship is to furnish it with what it needs.

indicatorNotes.Cycling: the last letter cycles round to the front

blocks.note: takes = demands, as in 'it takes courage'
the S moves from the back to the front

annotation.surface: A warning that the demands of cycling are dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' is the sport in the surface and an instruction to rotate letters in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to put money on a bet is to risk it.

entries.clue: Count on this church not in a god (6)

indicatorNotes.not in: the church is not in the god's name any more

annotation.surface: A believer told not to trust in a god outside the church.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Count on' looks like trust, relying on a god; it means counting, and an abacus is what you count on.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint: the bead frame is something you literally count on.

entries.clue: A familiar idea, smuggling in a drug (8)

indicatorNotes.smuggling: the trope smuggles IN inside itself

blocks.note: a trope is a familiar theme or device

annotation.surface: A well-worn plot device: someone smuggling drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like part of 'smuggling in'; it is the letters IN, smuggled into TROPE.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the alkaloid from deadly nightshade is a drug used to dilate pupils.

entries.clue: Swim to exercise round English Channel port (6)

indicatorNotes.round: the swim goes round the E

annotation.surface: A cross-Channel swim as a training exercise to reach a French port.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures swimming the English Channel, but English only gives E, and the Channel port is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Normandy town is a ferry port on the English Channel.

blocks.note: a sportsperson who has represented Oxford or Cambridge against the other, named for the university colours
risqué or smutty, as in a comedian's near-the-knuckle jokes

annotation.surface: A Cambridge sportsman coming off the field muddy.
annotation.walkthrough: A Blue is someone who has played for Oxford or Cambridge against the other; 'dirty' is the smutty kind, not muddy.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a Cambridge sportsman awarded university colours, and the old slang for indecent, as in films for adults.

indicatorNotes.on the radio: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is taken by sound

annotation.surface: The leading advertisement on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Main spot' reads as a top advertising slot; 'the main' is an old word for the open ocean.
annotation.definitionFit: An old poetic sense: 'the main' is the open ocean, as in the Spanish Main.
